scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to lie to my brother about having Asperger's syndrome for the rest of our lives. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My brother is two years younger than me and has Asperger's. We've known about it for years, but it's not something we talk about much in our family because he's embarrassed. He's extremely smart, excels in math and physics, and is doing well in college. Lately, he's been really depressed, even to the point of attempting suicide a couple of months ago. He called me in a panic, and I took him to the hospital. After that, he went through outpatient treatment. The nurse at the hospital mentioned that he shows signs of autism, which made me talk to him about it again. He's still denying it, but I know he's struggling with his self-image. I love him a lot, and he looks up to me. I want to help him feel better about himself, especially since his communication skills sometimes make his disorder obvious. I thought maybe if I told him I have Asperger's too, he might feel less alone and stop denying his own condition. But I'm wondering if that's a good idea or if I'd be being a jerk by lying to him for the rest of our lives. First, I need to consider the potential benefits of lying. If I tell him I have Asperger's, he might feel more connected to me and less isolated. It could help him accept his own diagnosis and maybe even seek help or be more open about it. He admires people like Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs, who are sometimes said to have Asperger's, so maybe seeing me embrace it would help him. On the other hand, lying could have serious consequences. If he finds out I lied, he might feel betrayed, which could damage our relationship. Trust is really important, especially between siblings. Also, lying about something as personal as a diagnosis might make him question other things I've told him, which could lead to bigger issues down the line. I also need to think about whether there are other ways to help him without lying. Maybe I can find other examples or role models who have Asperger's and are successful. I could encourage him to seek support groups or talk to a therapist who specializes in autism. Building his self-esteem through other means might be more effective and honest. Another thing to consider is how he feels about the diagnosis. He's denying it, which might be a defense mechanism because he's embarrassed or doesn't understand it yet. Pushing him to accept it, even through a lie, might not be the best approach. He might need time and space to come to terms with it on his own. I also wonder about the long-term effects of lying. If I lie about having Asperger's, would that affect how I see myself? It might cause internal conflict or stress if I have to maintain that lie over time. Plus, if he ever does accept his diagnosis, he might still feel the need to talk to someone about it, and I wouldn't be able to relate in the way he expects. Maybe instead of lying, I can be more supportive in other ways. I can listen to him without judgment, encourage him to express his feelings, and help him find resources that might make him feel better about himself. Building his confidence and showing him that his intelligence and achievements are what matter could help him move forward without the need for a lie. I also need to think about the ethical implications. Lying, even with good intentions, can be seen as wrong because it's not truthful. It might solve a short-term problem but create bigger issues in the future. Trust is hard to rebuild once it's broken, so I have to weigh the potential benefits against the risks. In summary, while the intention behind lying is to help my brother feel less alone, the potential negative consequences, such as betrayal and damage to our relationship, seem too significant. It might be better to find honest ways to support him, whether through encouragement, providing resources, or helping him find a community where he feels accepted. That way, I can be truthful and still be the supportive brother he needs.
